div.p: To engineer reliable real-time systems, it is desirable to detect timing anomalies early in the development process. However, there is little work addressing the problem of accurately predicting timing properties of real-time systems before implementations are developed. This paper describes an approach t o the specijication and schedulability analysis of real-time systems based on the timed process algebra ACSR-VP, which is an extension of ACSR with value-passing communication and dynamic priorities. Combined with the existing features of ACSR for representing time, synchronization and resource requirements, ACSR-VP is capable of specifying a variety of real-time systems with different scheduling disciplines in a modular fashion. Moreover, we can perform schedulability analysis on real-time systems specified in ACSR-VP automatically b y checking for a certain bisimulation relation.

div.head: I Introduction
div.p: As computers become ubiquitous, they are increasingly used in safety critical environments. Typical safety critical applications are control systems (manufacturing systems, avionics, robotics, intelligent highways, nuclear reactor systems), monitoring systems (patient monitoring, air traffic) and communication systems. Any failure of such computer systems may cause a great financial loss, environmental disaster or even the loss of lives. Potential high cost associated with an incorrect operation of these systems has created a demand for a rigorous framework in which various design alternatives can be formally specified and rigorously analyzed and tested before implementation.

One aspect common to all the safety critical sys- tems is that they must respond under stringent realtime constraints. That is, their correctness depends iiot only on how concurrent processes interact, but also on the time at which these interactions occur. There has been significant progress in the development of real-time formal methods that can be used to reason about real-time properties. Much of this work falls into the traditional categories of untimed *This research was supportedin p a t by NSF CCR 93-11622. NSF CCR 94-15346 and ARO DAAH04-95-1-0092. systems such as temporal logics, assertional methods, net-based models, automata theory and process algebras. While most formal models for real-time systems capture delays due to process synchronization, they abstract out resource-specific details by assuming idealistic operating environments.

On the other hand, there has been much work on schedulability analysis that addresses the problem of determining whether or not a real-time system under a particular scheduling discipline will meet its deadlines. The salient aspect of schedulability analysis is its ability to capture contention and scheduling of shared resources. However, the underlying computation model is generally limited to simple interactions between tasks. In addition, since some of schedulability results identify only sufficient conditions, a given set of tasks may be schedulable although they do not satisfy any schedulability conditions.

The goal of the approach described in this paper is to provide a formal framework based on process algebra in which one can carry out schedulability analysis during the development of design specifications. The advantage is that by incorporating schedulability analysis during the design specification phase, one can detect timing anomalies early in the development process. We note that too much detailed scheduling consideration during the design phase can make the design process unwieldy. On the other hand, if one does not consider scheduling factors at all, the analysis of a design may be useless since its predicted temporal behaviors may later turn out to be unrealizable. It would be fruitful to develop an iterative software engineering methodology such as [9], which can be followed to eventually determine necessary level of scheduling consideration at the design phase. This paper describes a formal framework that can accommodate such a methodology.

The framework described in this paper is based on a timed process algebra, called Algebra of Communicating Shared Resources (ACSR) [16]. ACSR is a formalism that has language level support for specifying synchronization, resource contention, static priority mechanisms of real-time systems. We have also developed a toolkit based on ACSR, which has been successfully applied to specification and analysis of a number of well-known examples [17, 41. In this paper, we extend ACSR, called ACSR-VP (ACSR Value Passing) with value-passing communication and dynamic priorities, and illustrate how to use it to specify and analyze priority-driven real-time systems. ACSR-VP can model, in a modular fashion, a wide range of real-time systems consisting of preemptive or non-preemptive, periodic or aperiodic, independent or dependent tasks running on single 011 multiple processors. Also, various static-priority and dynamicpriority scheduling disciplines can be incorporated into the ACSR-VP task models. Once a particular task model together with its scheduling discipline has been modeled as finite-state ACSR-VP processes, it is simple to do schedulability analysis. In fact, schedulability analysis reduces to bisimulation checking on ACSR-VP processes, which can be carried out automatically for finite-state processes.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Related work on formal methods in schedulability analysis and value-passing process algebras is reviewed in Section 2. Section 3 introduces the syntax and semantics of ACSR-VP. Section 4 systematically demonstrates how to specify different task models and scheduling disciplines using ACSR-VP. The analysis, especially schedulability analysis, of ACSR-VP specifications of real-time systems is discussed in Section 5. The paper is concluded with Section 6.

div.head: Relat8ed Work
div.p: The pioineering work by Liu and Layland [lS] derives schedulability conditions for rake monotonic (RMd scheduling and earliest-deadline-first (EDF) sche uling. Since then, much work on schedulability analysis hat; been done which includes .various extensions of these results [26, 24, 3, 25, 22, 1.9, 11. Each of the extensions expands the applicabili.ty of schedulability analysis by allowing different task models. However, these 'task models are still based on simple computation m'odels compared to what 0u.r approach allows.

There is relatively little work on the specification and analysis of real-time scheduling based on formal methods. Burns and Wellings [a] present a formal treatment of the basic priority inheritance protocol using the combined notation of Occam and Z. Occam is used to s,pecify processes whereas Z is used to describe the scheduling of Occam processes based on the priority inheritance protocol. The emphasis of this work is to study the properties and implementation issues of the protocol, rather than schedulability analysis. Gerber and Lee [lo] describe our previous work on schedulability analysis based on a timed process algebra. The process algebra used is the predecessor of ACSR which has limited features and does not support dynamic priorities, Fredette and Cleaveland [8] describe an interesting, but different, approach to schedulability analysis based on process algebra. The main difference is that their process algebra does not support the notions of resources, priorities and synchronization, hence has limited expressibility. Consequently, iz real-time scheduling discipline has to be specified using a functional notation that is not part of the process algebra used to describe real-time tasks.

Therefore, schedulability analysis cannot be done using the analysis techniques of the underlying process algebra. According to the paper, there are some limitations on what task models it can handle without extending the notation. Corbett [7] describes an approach based on timed automata augmented with prioritized transitions. The approach is to translate Ada tasks executed by a preemptive priority scheduler into timed automata and apply a semi-decision procedure for proving timing properties of the Ada tasks.

An excellent account of extendin process algebra with value-passing can be found inI201. Since then, several formal semantics, equivalence relations and associated proof systems for value-passing CCS have been developed [27, 11, 131. In particular, Hennessy and Lin [12] and Schreiber [23] develop symbolic approaches to bisimulation for value-passing. Cleaveland and Yankelevich [6] provide an alternative operational semantics for value-passing CCS with emphasis on implementability of the semantics. div.p: In this section, we demonstrate that ACSR-VP can be used to model a variety of real-time systems under different scheduling disciplines. We first show how to specify the behavior of individual tasks with different attributes using ACSR-VP. Then, we show how to incorporate specific scheduling disciplines and, thus, model behavior of task systems running in realistic environment using ACSR-VP.

In the traditional approaches to schedulability analysis, the process of analyzing schedulability of a realtime system usually consists of a number of different procedures that perform exhaustive simulation or st,ate space exploration on task systems. Applicability of any of these procedures is limited to specific system chara.cteristics. The approach proposed in this paper is more general in the sense that schedulability analysis of any real-time systems specified using ACSR-VP reduces to the bisimulation checking problem stated as Equation (1) of Lemma5.1. The truth of Equation (1) can be solved using the existing algorithms, and thus obviating the need of developing different analysis procedures for different system characteristics.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We have described the use of the process algebra as a general framework to specify and analyze real-time systems. In particular, we extend the timed process algebra ACSR with value-passing and dynamic priorities. The extended process algebra, ACSR-VP, is capable of specifying realistic characteristics of real-time systems, as well as different scheduling disciplines. We have introduced the specification methodology of using ACSR-VP to write a real-time task model including a scheduling discipline. Furthermore, we described how to perform schedulability analysis using bisimulation checking of ACSR-VP processes.

The novel feature of our approach is that schedulability of real-time systems can be formulated formally and analyzed automatically, all in the framework of process algebra. It has been often criticized that scheduling work is not very well integrated with other aspects of real-time system development [l]. Our work is a step toward such an intergration, which helps to meet our goal of making ACSR a useful formalism that supports the development of reliable real-time systems.

There are several issues that should be investigated. For example, it remains to study how to directly check bisimulation relations on ACSR-VP processes without translating to ACSR processes. We are also interested in developing other analysis techniques for ACSR-VP such as rewriting and testing. Furthermore, it would be useful if we can formulate and solve the synthesis problems of determining feasible or optimal scheduling given timing requirements in the framework of ACSR. Finally, we need to implement the proposed approach in VERSA more efficiently using techniques for alleviating the state explosion problem such as BDDs and state minimization algorithms [15], and apply it to realistic real-time systems to evaluate its benefits and limitations.

div.p: The above examples illustrate how to specify various task models using ACSR-VP. In the next subsection, we demonstrate how to incorporate various scheduling disciplines into task models specified using ACSIL-VP.

div.head: Scheduling Disciplines
div.p: Scheduling of Independent Tasks. Having specified the task models using ACSR-VP in the way shown in the last subsection, we only need to assign proper priorities to the timed actions in the ACSR processes to reflect the scheduling discipline used for independent tasks. As an example, we present a complete specification of a task system scheduled by ear[zest-deadlzne-Jirst (EDF). EDF is a dynamicpriority scheduling algorithm in which an uncompleted job with earlier deadline has higher priority.
